To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children imitate gestures more accurately when the gestures are common targets in a nursery game than when the gestures are uncommon targets in a nursery games.

2- and-3-year-old children imitated more when the modeled gesture was topographically similar to a common gesture in nursery matching games than when the modeled gesture resembled an uncommon one, and that they imitated more with their dominant hand.

children imitate more often to models of common gestures than uncommon ones, and that they are more likely to respond to a common gesture as a match than as a mismatch, but they are equally likely to produce matching responses to a common or an uncommon model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
imitation in children and the factors that determine whether they will imitate a gesture.
the development of imitation in children.
the determinants of imitation of novel gestures in young children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results are consistent with both accounts.

the children's imitation of gestures was determined by a number of factors, including: (1) the similarity of the model and response, (2) the similarity of model and response in terms of the game in which they were used, (3) the similarity of response to the model in terms of the side of the body on which it was performed, (4) the side of the model's response, and (5) the age of the child.

the data are consistent with a model in which the child's imitation of a gesture is determined by the relative strength of two factors--the similarity of the target gesture to a gesture in the child's repertoire and the similarity of the target to the gestures with which the child is familiar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children's imitation of hand-to-face gestures is determined by a complex interaction of topography, training history and response bias.
imitation is an important part of the social learning process and that children are more likely to imitate a behavior that has been reinforced than one that has not.
children are sensitive to a variety of factors that influence their imitative responses, and that these factors are not always consistent with cognitive goal theories of imitation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the imitation of gestures is influenced by a number of factors, such as the similarity between the gesture and the target and the child's familiarity with the gesture.
the imitation of hand-to body gestures by young children is a complex process that is sensitive to a variety of topographical, social, and environmental factors.

young children are sensitive to the social and environmental contingencies that surround their learning experiences, and that this is true even when the learning experience is as simple as playing a game.
